summary: An FYI that collects the questions school communities most commonly ask about the Internet and points to sources that answer them. It was replaced by RFC 1941.

eli5.summary: A question-and-answer sheet for teachers and students who are new to the Internet.

questions: fyi for primary and secondary school users
how to connect schools to internet
subtitle: A Q&A guide for schools connecting to the Internet

tldr.problem: Teachers, administrators and students in primary and secondary schools wanted to use the Internet but lacked guidance on how to get connected, what equipment to buy, and how to use it safely and effectively in classrooms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1578 collects the most frequently asked questions from school communities and provides answers with pointers to resources for Internet connectivity, tools, educational projects, and security practices.
tldr.outcome: The document served as a practical guide for schools navigating early Internet adoption. It was replaced by RFC 1941 as the Internet landscape and school technology evolved.

today: RFC 1578 is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1941 in May 1996, which updated the answers for the evolving Internet landscape. The fundamental questions remain relevant, but the technologies, costs, and resources available have changed significantly.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1578 is an FYI document that compiles the most common questions asked by educators, administrators, and students in primary and secondary schools about the Internet. The document was produced by the Internet School Networking group within the Internet Engineering Task Force. It acknowledges that school communities face unique challenges when adopting Internet technology: they have less technical expertise and fewer resources than universities or government agencies, and they must address concerns specific to students and parents.

The RFC emphasizes that the Internet is volatile and constantly changing, so it focuses on stable services and provides pointers to other resources rather than trying to be comprehensive. It was intended as a practical guide for schools considering or beginning to use Internet connectivity.
sections.eli5: Schools asked lots of questions about getting online. This document collected the most common ones and answered them clearly.

sections.title: Benefits and Challenges for Schools
sections.content:
The RFC describes the potential benefits of Internet access for classrooms. These include access to worldwide information resources, connection with experts and educators globally, support for curriculum improvement and school reform, and tools to reduce the isolation many teachers experience. The document also acknowledges the practical challenges: educators must find time to learn new tools, schools must convince administrators to fund connections, and technical support must be in place to keep systems running reliably.

The cost of Internet connections varied depending on the type of service desired, ranging from low-end dial-up access (approximately USD 100 to 800 plus monthly fees) to high-speed dedicated lines for entire schools (USD 2,000 to 3,000 plus monthly fees of at least 200). The RFC discusses three connection scenarios and recommends that schools consider their specific needs before purchasing equipment.
sections.eli5: The Internet lets students find information and talk to people around the world, but it costs money and schools need trained people to help it work.

sections.title: Security and Ethical Use
sections.content:
The RFC addresses several safety and security concerns specific to schools. One major concern was that students might access inappropriate material. The document explains that purely technical solutions cannot prevent this on a direct Internet connection, but schools can use filtering approaches like store-and-forward systems that give them some control over content. More importantly, the RFC recommends that schools develop clear policies governing Internet use and integrate ethics and technology into the curriculum so students learn responsible behavior.

The document also discusses computer security. It distinguishes between hackers (skilled computer people) and crackers (people who illegally break into systems). Schools must protect their own computers and teach students about responsible conduct. The RFC recommends obtaining security software and following proper authentication and access control procedures, pointing to resources like the Site Security Handbook (FYI 8) for detailed guidance.
sections.eli5: Schools need rules about what students can do online, and they need to protect computers from people trying to break in. Teaching students ethics is important too.

sections.title: Getting Connected: Technical Options
sections.content:
The RFC describes several approaches to getting Internet access. Local area networks (LANs) with dedicated Internet connections serve multiple computers but require more initial equipment investment. Dial-up access using modems is cheaper initially but limits the number of simultaneous users. The document mentions store-and-forward systems like UUCP, FrEdMail, FidoNet, and K12Net as alternatives that work over regular phone lines but with delayed message delivery, offering more affordable access and content filtering capabilities.

The RFC recommends involving dedicated technical staff, using the train-the-trainer model for user education, and sourcing help from local colleges, universities, technology companies, and community networks. It emphasizes that staff training is often the most neglected aspect of technology plans but is critical for success.
sections.eli5: Schools can connect different ways: direct connections are fast but expensive, dial-up is cheaper, and special email networks are even cheaper but slower.

sections.title: Resources and Support
sections.content:
The RFC provides extensive contact information for organizations supporting school networking, including the Consortium for School Networking (CoSN), Kidsphere mailing list, Ednet, KIDLINK, and others. It lists electronic bulletin board systems, gopher servers, telnet services, and newsgroups where educators can find help, discuss projects, and share lesson plans.

The document references guides and tools for finding information on the Internet, including Archie for file searching, Gopher for menu-based information retrieval, and WAIS (Wide Area Information Server) for keyword searching. It also provides bibliography of books on the Internet, FYI documents, and information about obtaining RFCs. The extensive appendices cover how to retrieve documents electronically via FTP and Gopher, and provide a glossary of Internet terms.
sections.eli5: There are lots of mailing lists and servers where teachers can get help, find projects to do with students, and learn more about the Internet.
